definition: Coronary artery disease (also called coronary heart disease) is the most common type of heart disease in both men and women. In the United States, heart disease is the number one cause of death in women. But women are often not diagnosed with heart disease as quickly as men are. That's because: Women are more likely than men to have "silent" heart disease, meaning that they don't have symptoms. A delay in diagnosis may mean a delay in medical care that could help prevent serious problems, such as a heart attack. That's why it's important to learn about your risk for heart disease, the symptoms in women, and how to keep your heart healthy. Like men, the most common type of heart disease among women is coronary artery disease. But there are certain types of heart disease which are less common, but affect women more often than men: Coronary microvascular disease - Chest pain from spasms (sudden tightening) in the smallest arteries of the heart that pinch off blood flow. That's why women generally develop coronary artery disease 10 years later than men. Remember, women can have heart disease without symptoms. But if you pay attention to your risk for heart disease, you can take action to prevent problems or keep them from getting worse.
symptoms: Health care providers may not recognize heart disease in women. Women's symptoms may be different from men's symptoms.
risk_factors: You can help lower your risk by learning how to prevent heart disease and making heart-healthy habits part of your daily life.

What is heart surgery? Heart surgery can correct certain heart problems when other treatments haven't worked or can't be used. In some cases, heart surgery may be a medical emergency. For example, surgery for a severe heart attack may need to be done right away. A heart-lung bypass machine keeps oxygen-rich blood pumping through the body during the surgery. Surgeons may use off-pump heart surgery to do coronary artery bypass grafts (CABG), but only in certain cases. Minimally invasive heart surgery uses small cuts between the ribs. This type of heart surgery may or may not use a heart-lung bypass machine. This allows the surgeon to be very accurate when doing difficult operations. What are the risks of heart surgery? Like all surgery, heart surgery has risks even though the results are often excellent. The risks include: Bleeding Infection, fever , and swelling A problem from anesthesia (medicine that makes you sleep during surgery) Arrhythmia Damage to the heart, kidneys, liver, and lungs Stroke The risks of heart surgery tend to be higher if: The surgery is an emergency.

definition: The good news is that you can often prevent or treat high blood pressure. Some medicines can raise your blood pressure, including: Certain antidepressants Decongestants (medicines to relieve a stuffy nose) Hormonal birth control pills Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), which are a type of pain reliever Having certain other medical conditions, such as: Some tumors Chronic kidney disease Diabetes Metabolic syndrome Overweight and obesity Sleep apnea Thyroid problems How can I prevent high blood pressure? You can help prevent high blood pressure by having a healthy lifestyle. Regular physical activity can help you maintain a healthy weight and lower your blood pressure. Maintaining a healthy weight can help you control high blood pressure and reduce your risk for other health problems. Learning how to relax and manage stress can improve your emotional and physical health and lower high blood pressure. Getting enough high-quality sleep . They work by killing the bacteria or by making it hard for the bacteria to grow and multiply. Antibiotics only treat certain bacterial infections, such as strep throat, urinary tract infections , and E. coli . Some of the common side effects include: Rash Nausea Diarrhea Yeast infections More serious side effects can include: C. diff infections , which cause diarrhea that can lead to severe colon damage and sometimes even death Severe and life-threatening allergic reactions Antibiotic resistance infections Call your health care provider if you develop any side effects while taking your antibiotic. Why is it important to take antibiotics only when they're needed? You should only take antibiotics when they are needed because they can cause side effects and can contribute to antibiotic resistance . Antibiotic resistance happens when the bacteria change and become able to resist the effects of an antibiotic.
treatment: When you take antibiotics, it is important that you take them responsibly. Always follow the directions carefully.

definition: Antidepressants are prescription medicines to treat depression. A health care provider may prescribe antidepressants for anxiety , chronic pain , or insomnia . Sometimes providers also prescribe antidepressants for other conditions. Most of the newer antidepressants belong to one of these three groups: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) Serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors (SNRIs) Atypical antidepressants, which are newer antidepressants that don't fit into the other groups If these antidepressants don't help, your provider might suggest one of the older antidepressants. The older types include tricyclic antidepressants (TCAs), tetracyclics, and monoamine oxidase inhibitors (MAOIs). An antidepressant that helped a parent, brother, or sister could be a good choice for you, too. Certain antidepressants can make some other conditions better or worse. How long do antidepressants take to work? Antidepressants usually take 4 to 8 weeks to work, so you'll need to be patient. But if you do have them, they're usually mild and may get better over time as your body gets used to the new medicine. If you have any side effects from antidepressants, your provider may suggest ways to manage them while you wait to see if the antidepressant will work.
symptoms: Some antidepressants may do a better job helping specific symptoms, such as trouble sleeping. Some antidepressants may help specific symptoms such as sleep problems.
treatment: A health care provider may prescribe antidepressants for anxiety, chronic pain or insomnia. The typical length of treatment is 6 to 12 months, but some people may stay on antidepressants for much longer.
risk_factors: The most common side effects from antidepressants include: Nausea and vomiting, weight gain, and sexual problems. Even though these antidepressants may cause more serious side effects, the benefits may outweigh the risks.

definition: What is anxiety? Anxiety is a feeling of fear, dread, and uneasiness. What are the types of anxiety disorders? There are several types of anxiety disorders, including: Generalized anxiety disorder (GAD). People with GAD worry about ordinary issues such as health, money, work, and family. But their worries are excessive, and they have them almost every day for at least 6 months. The cause of anxiety is unknown. The risk factors for the different types of anxiety disorders can vary. For example, GAD and phobias are more common in women, but social anxiety affects men and women equally. The different types of anxiety disorders can have different symptoms. But they all have a combination of: Anxious thoughts or beliefs that are hard to control. How are anxiety disorders diagnosed? To diagnose anxiety disorders, your health care provider will ask about your symptoms and medical history. The main treatments for anxiety disorders are psychotherapy (talk therapy), medicines, or both: Psychotherapy can help you recognize and change troubling emotions, thoughts, and behaviors. There are many types; some of the types used for anxiety disorders include: Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), which teaches you different ways of thinking and behaving. It can help you change how you react to the things that cause you to feel fear and anxiety. Acceptance and commitment therapy may help with some anxiety disorders. Medicines to treat anxiety disorders include anti-anxiety medicines and certain antidepressants . Some types of medicines may work better for specific types of anxiety disorders.
symptoms: To diagnose anxiety disorders, your health care provider will ask about your symptoms and medical history. There are some general risk factors for all types of anxiety disorders. Certain personality traits, such as being shy or withdrawn when you are in new situations or meeting new people, are also risk factors.
diagnosis: How are anxiety disorders diagnosed?  How do you know if you have an anxiety disorder? What are the symptoms? How are you diagnosed?
treatment: Psychotherapy can help you recognize and change troubling emotions, thoughts, and behaviors. Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) teaches you different ways of thinking and behaving. Acceptance and commitment therapy may help with some anxiety disorders.
risk_factors: The risk factors for the different types of anxiety disorders can vary. Who is at risk for anxiety disorders?

What is asthma? Asthma is a chronic (long-term) lung disease. When you have asthma, your airways can become inflamed and narrowed. An asthma trigger is something that can set off or worsen your asthma symptoms. Different triggers can cause different types of asthma: Allergic asthma is caused by allergens. Your provider may adjust your treatment until asthma symptoms are controlled. Sometimes asthma is severe and cannot be controlled with other treatments.
symptoms: An asthma trigger is something that can set off or worsen your asthma symptoms. These symptoms can range from mild to severe. When these symptoms get worse than usual, it is called an asthma attack.
diagnosis: Lung function tests, including spirometry, to test how well your lungs work.Tests to measure how your airways react to specific exposures.
treatment: Sometimes asthma is severe and cannot be controlled with other treatments. If you are having asthma attacks, you may need a change in your treatment.
risk_factors: Being exposed to secondhand smoke when your mother is pregnant with you or when you are a small child can raise your risk of having asthma. Black and African Americans and Puerto Ricans are at higher risk.

definition: Your immune system can tell that the germs aren't part of you, so it destroys them. If you have an autoimmune disease, your immune system attacks the healthy cells of your organs and tissues by mistake. Who is at risk for autoimmune diseases? Millions of Americans of all ages have autoimmune diseases. That's because many autoimmune diseases have similar symptoms. And some symptoms, such as muscle aches, are common in many other illnesses. What are the treatments for autoimmune diseases?
symptoms: The symptoms of an autoimmune disease depend on the part of your body that's affected. Many types of autoimmune diseases cause redness, swelling, heat, and pain.
diagnosis: Doctors often have a hard time diagnosing autoimmune diseases. How are autoimmune diseases diagnosed?

What is birth control? Birth control, also known as contraception, is the use of medicines, devices, or surgery to prevent pregnancy. What are the different types of birth control? There are several different types of birth control, and they work in different ways: Barrier methods Male condom A thin sheath that covers the penis to collect sperm and prevent it from entering the woman's body. Hormonal methods Oral contraceptives ("the pill") Pills that a woman takes every day. The woman inserts the ring into the vagina, where it continually releases hormones for three weeks. Injectable birth control An injection of a hormone that a woman gets once every three months. Long-acting reversible contraceptives (LARCs) Intrauterine device (IUD) A small, T-shaped device that a provider inserts into the uterus. What are some other forms of pregnancy prevention? There are some types of pregnancy prevention that do not involve medicines, devices, or surgery: Other forms of pregnancy prevention Fertility awareness-based methods They are also called natural rhythm methods. They involve tracking the woman's fertility cycle and avoiding sex or using barrier methods on the days when she is most likely to get pregnant. Lactational amenorrhea method (LAM) A form of natural birth control for breastfeeding mothers.
risk_factors: When deciding which birth control type is right for you, there are many different factors to consider. Your provider can answer your questions about birth control to help you select the best type.

definition: A birth defect is a problem that happens while a baby is developing in the mother's body. Some birth defects like cleft lip or neural tube defects are structural problems that can be easy to see. Birth defects can range from mild to severe. What are the treatments for birth defects? Children with birth defects often need special care and treatments. Can birth defects be prevented? Not all birth defects can be prevented. But there are things you can do before and during pregnancy to increase your chance of having a healthy baby: Start prenatal care as soon as you think you might be pregnant, and see your health care provider regularly during pregnancy Get 400 micrograms (mcg) of folic acid every day.
symptoms: The symptoms and problems caused by birth defects vary. Because of this, the treatments also vary. For more information on birth defects click here.
diagnosis: Being an older mother, typically over the age of 34 years, can increase your risk of having a baby with a birth defect. Health care providers can diagnose some birth defects using prenatal testing.
treatment: Start prenatal care as soon as you think you might be pregnant. See your health care provider regularly during pregnancy. Get 400 micrograms (mcg) of folic acid every day.
risk_factors: Researchers think that most birth defects are caused by a complex mix of factors, which can include:Genetics.

What are blisters? Blisters are fluid-filled sacs on the outer layer of your skin. Other names for blisters are vesicles (usually for smaller blisters) and bulla (for larger blisters). What causes blisters? Blisters often happen when there is friction - rubbing or pressure - on one spot. Can blisters be prevented? There are some things you can do to prevent friction blisters: Make sure that your shoes fit properly Always wear socks with your shoes, and make sure that the socks fit well. You may want to wear socks that are acrylic or nylon, so they keep moisture away from your feet.
treatment: Blisters will usually heal on their own. Other causes of blisters include:Burns, frostbite, and allergic reactions. You should contact your health care provider if you have blisters.

definition: Your body breaks down most of that food into glucose and releases it into your bloodstream. Over time, having too much glucose in your blood can cause serious health problems (diabetes complications). When and how should I check my blood glucose? If you have diabetes, you'll likely need to check your blood glucose every day to make sure that your blood glucose numbers are in your target range. Some people may need to check their blood glucose several times a day. The sensor measures your glucose level every few minutes. It can show changes in your glucose level throughout the day and night. High blood glucose may also be caused by other conditions that can affect insulin or glucose levels in your blood. For many people with diabetes, this means a blood glucose reading lower than 70 mg/dL. Your number might be different, so check with your health care team to find out what blood glucose level is low for you. Symptoms of low blood glucose tend to come on quickly. Low blood glucose can be dangerous and should be treated as soon as possible. Although it's rare, you can still get low blood glucose without having diabetes. See your provider to find out the cause of your low blood glucose and how to treat it.

definition: What are blood thinners? Blood thinners are medicines that prevent blood clots from forming. There are different types of blood thinners: Anticoagulants, such as heparin or warfarin (also called Coumadin), slow down your body's process of making clots. How can I take blood thinners safely? When you take a blood thinner, follow the directions carefully. Blood thinners may interact with certain foods, medicines, vitamins, and alcohol. What are the side effects of blood thinners? Bleeding is the most common side effect of blood thinners.
treatment: When you take a blood thinner, follow the directions carefully.  How can I take blood thinners safely?
risk_factors: You may need a blood thinner if you have:Certain heart or blood vessel diseases. An abnormal heart rhythm called atrial fibrillation. A heart valve replacement. A risk of blood clots after surgery.Congenital heart defects.

Cardiac rehabilitation (rehab) is a medically supervised program to help people who have: A heart attack Angioplasty or coronary artery bypass grafting for coronary heart disease A heart valve repair or replacement A heart transplant or a lung transplant Angina Heart failure The goal is to help you return to an active life, and to reduce the risk of further heart problems.
risk_factors: The goal is to help you return to an active life, and to reduce the risk of further heart problems. Cardiac rehabilitation (rehab) is a medically supervised program.

definition: Researchers aren't sure whether long-term typing or computer use leads to carpal tunnel syndrome. Carpal tunnel syndrome usually happens only in adults. The next step would be treatments for carpal tunnel syndrome.
symptoms: You may feel numbness, tingling or burning in your fingers, especially in your thumb, index, and middle fingers. Carpal tunnel syndrome rarely comes back after surgery, but mild symptoms may last.
diagnosis: How is carpal tunnel syndrome diagnosed? How is it treated? What are the symptoms and how are they treated?
treatment: It's easier to treat carpal tunnel syndrome early on, so you should start treatment as soon as possible. Some people may find acupuncture and chiropractic care helpful, but research hasn't shown that these therapies can improve carpal Tunnel Syndrome.

Cholesterol is a waxy, fat-like substance that's found in all the cells in your body. What are HDL, LDL, and VLDL? HDL, LDL, and VLDL are lipoproteins. Some people also call VLDL a "bad" cholesterol because it too contributes to the buildup of plaque in your arteries. This lowers your HDL (good) cholesterol. Smoking , which lowers HDL cholesterol, especially in women. Other medical conditions and certain medicines may also raise LDL cholesterol levels or lower HDL cholesterol levels. What can raise my risk of high cholesterol? A variety of things can raise your risk of high cholesterol: Age. For example, Asian Americans are more likely to have high levels of LDL cholesterol than other groups. What other health problems can high cholesterol cause? Undiagnosed or untreated high blood cholesterol can lead to serious health problems: If you have large deposits of plaque in your arteries, an area of plaque can rupture (break open). This treatment uses a filtering machine to remove LDL cholesterol from the blood.
symptoms: There are usually no signs or symptoms that you have high cholesterol. How is high cholesterol diagnosed?
diagnosis: Undiagnosed or untreated high blood cholesterol can lead to serious health problems. If you have large deposits of plaque in your arteries, an area of plaque can rupture (break open)
treatment: Certain medicines can raise your level of LDL cholesterol. These include: Steroids, chemotherapy and certain acne medicines. Lipoprotein apheresis is a treatment for familial hypercholesterolemia.
risk_factors: Between ages 20 and 39, men have a greater risk of high total cholesterol than women. People from certain racial or ethnic groups may have an increased risk. Conditions such as diabetes, chronic kidney disease and HIV can raise your risk.

definition: Cholesterol numbers are measured in milligrams per deciliter (mg/dL). Levels less than 40 mg/dL are considered low. Women age 20 or older: Type of Cholesterol Healthy Level Total Cholesterol Less than 200 mg/dL Non-HDL Less than 130 mg/dL LDL Less than 100 mg/dL HDL Greater than or equal to 60 mg/dL is best. Levels less than 50 mg/dL are considered low. Cigarette smoking lowers your HDL cholesterol. Some factors that you cannot change can also affect cholesterol levels, such as: Age. For example, Asian Americans are more likely to have high levels of LDL cholesterol than other groups. And non-Hispanic White people are more likely than other groups to have high levels of total cholesterol.

When deciding which medicine you should take and which dose you need, your provider will consider: Your cholesterol levels.

What is circumcision? Circumcision is a surgical procedure to remove the foreskin from the penis. In the United States, circumcision is often done before a new baby leaves the hospital. What should I consider when deciding whether to have my baby circumcised? As parents, it is your decision whether to have your baby circumcised. What are the medical benefits of circumcision? The possible medical benefits of circumcision include: A lower risk of HIV and some other sexually transmitted infections (STIs). Easier hygiene. What are the risks of circumcision? The risks of circumcision include: A low risk of bleeding, infection, or scarring.

The air sacs fill up with air, like a small balloon. When you breathe out, the air sacs deflate, and the air goes out. If you have COPD, less air flows in and out of your airways because of one or more problems: The airways and air sacs in your lungs become less elastic The walls between many of the air sacs are destroyed The walls of the airways become thick and inflamed The airways make more mucus than usual and can become clogged What are the types of COPD (chronic obstructive pulmonary disease)? Most people with COPD have both emphysema and chronic bronchitis, but how severe each type is can be different from person to person. What causes COPD (chronic obstructive pulmonary disease)? The cause of COPD is usually long-term exposure to irritants that damage your lungs and airways. Exposure to other inhaled irritants can contribute to COPD. Who is at risk for COPD (chronic obstructive pulmonary disease)? What are the symptoms of COPD (chronic obstructive pulmonary disease)? How is COPD (chronic obstructive pulmonary disease) diagnosed? Your health care provider may use many tools to make a diagnosis: A medical history, which includes asking about your symptoms A family history Various tests, such as lung function tests , a chest x-ray or CT scan , and blood tests Your doctor will diagnose COPD based on your signs and symptoms, your medical and family histories, and test results. What are the treatments for COPD (chronic obstructive pulmonary disease)? There is no cure for COPD. Can COPD (chronic obstructive pulmonary disease) be prevented? Since smoking causes most cases of COPD, the best way to prevent it is to not smoke.
symptoms: Most people who have COPD are at least 40 years old when their symptoms begin. Your doctor will diagnose COPD based on your signs and symptoms. It's important to know when and where to get help for your symptoms.
diagnosis: How is COPD (chronic obstructive pulmonary disease) diagnosed? How is it diagnosed? What are the symptoms of COPD?
treatment: There is no cure for COPD. Vaccines for the flu and pneumococcal pneumonia, since people with COPD are at higher risk for serious problems from these diseases. Antibiotics if you get a bacterial or viral lung infection. Oxygen therapy if you have severe COPD
risk_factors: Smoking. People who have asthma have more risk of developing COPD than people who don't have asthma.

What is dementia? Dementia is a loss of mental functions that is severe enough to affect your daily life and activities. It is a serious disorder which interferes with your daily life. What are the types of dementia? The most common types of dementia are known as neurodegenerative disorders. They include: Alzheimer's disease , which is the most common form of dementia among older people. Lewy body dementia , which causes movement symptoms along with dementia. For example, some people have both Alzheimer's disease and vascular dementia. Dementia also causes problems with the ability to think, problem solve, and reason. For example, people with dementia may: Get lost in a familiar neighborhood Use unusual words to refer to familiar objects Forget the name of a close family member or friend Forget old memories Need help doing tasks that they used to do by themselves Some people with dementia cannot control their emotions and their personalities may change. Certain types of dementia can also cause problems with balance and movement. The stages of dementia range from mild to severe.
symptoms: The symptoms of dementia can vary, depending on which parts of the brain are affected. There is no cure for most types of dementia, including Alzheimer's disease and Lewy body dementia.
diagnosis: How is dementia diagnosed?  How is it diagnosed? How is dementia treated? What are the signs and symptoms of dementia? What is the diagnosis?
treatment: Mental health counseling to help people with dementia and their families learn how to manage difficult emotions and behaviors. Music or art therapy to reduce anxiety and improve well-being.
risk_factors: This is the biggest risk factor for dementia. Living a healthy lifestyle might influence some of your risk factors.

definition: Depression is a serious medical illness. Symptoms can include: Feeling sad or "empty" Loss of interest in favorite activities Overeating, or not wanting to eat at all Not being able to sleep, or sleeping too much Feeling very tired Feeling hopeless, irritable, anxious, or guilty Aches or pains, headaches, cramps, or digestive problems Thoughts of death or suicide Depression is a disorder of the brain. Depression is one part of bipolar disorder . There are effective treatments for depression, including antidepressants , talk therapy, or both.
symptoms: Depression is a disorder of the brain. Symptoms can include: feeling sad or "empty" or feeling hopeless, irritable, anxious, or guilty.
treatment: There are effective treatments for depression, including antidepressants , talk therapy, or both. There are also treatments for bipolar disorder, including medication.

A hormone called insulin helps the glucose get into your cells. Without enough insulin, glucose can't get into your cells as quickly as usual. People with type 1 diabetes need to take a diabetes medicine called insulin to control their blood sugar. What are the types of medicines for type 1 diabetes? If you have type 1 diabetes, you must take insulin because your body no longer makes it. There are different types of insulin that start to work at different speeds, and the effects of each last a different length of time. Some people with type 2 diabetes take both pills and injections.
With type 1 diabetes, your pancreas does not make insulin.

Type 2 diabetes may be caused by a combination of factors: Being overweight or having obesity Not being physically active Genetics and family history Type 2 diabetes usually starts with insulin resistance. What are the treatments for type 2 diabetes? Treatment for type 2 diabetes involves managing your blood sugar levels.

definition: Chronic diarrhea -- diarrhea that lasts at least four weeks -- can be a symptom of a chronic disease. Who is at risk for diarrhea? People of all ages can get diarrhea. Diarrhea can cause dehydration , which means that your body does not have enough fluid to work properly.
symptoms: Diarrhea lasting more than a few days may be a sign of a more serious problem. Chronic diarrhea -- diarrhea that lasts at least four weeks -- can be a symptom of a chronic disease. The most common causes of diarrhea include: bacteria from contaminated food or water.
diagnosis: How is the cause of diarrhea diagnosed?  How is it diagnosed? What is the best way to treat diarrhea? What are the symptoms of diarrhea?
treatment: Diarrhea is treated by replacing lost fluids and electrolytes to prevent dehydration. Use bottled or purified water for drinking, making ice cubes, and brushing your teeth. Make sure that the cooked food you eat is fully cooked and served hot.
risk_factors: If your diarrhea goes away within a few days, finding the cause is usually not necessary. People of all ages can get diarrhea.

definition: What are disabilities? A disability is any condition of your body or mind that makes it more difficult for you to do one or more major life activities and interact with the world around you.
treatment: Many people with disabilities report that their health is good or better. But they may have or be at risk of health problems related to their disability. These conditions may include:Bowel or bladder problems, chronic pain and heart disease.

definition: So sometimes Down syndrome is also called trisomy 21. Down syndrome is usually not inherited. One factor that increases the risk of having a baby with Down syndrome is the age of the mother. What are the treatments for Down syndrome? There is no single, standard treatment for Down syndrome. Since people with Down syndrome can have birth defects and other health problems, they will need regular medical care.
symptoms: The symptoms of Down syndrome are different in each person. People with Down syndrome may have different problems at different times of their lives. Some of the common physical signs of the syndrome include a flat face and short neck.
diagnosis: Prenatal diagnostic tests can diagnose or rule out Down syndrome. These tests check the chromosomes in a sample of cells.
treatment: Health care providers can check for Down syndrome during pregnancy or after a child is born. People with Down syndrome can have birth defects and other health problems.

Drug use, or misuse, includes: Using illegal substances, such as Anabolic steroids Club drugs Cocaine Heroin Inhalants Marijuana Methamphetamines Misusing prescription medicines , including opioids . Using the medicine for another purpose, such as getting high Misusing over-the-counter medicines, including using them for another purpose and using them in a different way than you are supposed to Drug use is dangerous. What is drug addiction? Drug addiction is a chronic brain disease. Repeated drug use can change the brain and lead to addiction. The brain changes from addiction can be lasting, so drug addiction is considered a "relapsing" disease. People who have untreated mental health problems , such as depression , anxiety , or attention deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) are more likely to become addicted. If you have a mental disorder along with an addiction, it is known as a dual diagnosis . Drug use and addiction are preventable.

Eczema is a term for several different types of skin swelling. Eczema is also called dermatitis. The cause of eczema is unknown. Eczema may get better or worse over time, but it is often a long-lasting disease. The most common type of eczema is atopic dermatitis.
Edema means swelling caused by fluid in your body's tissues.
treatment: Causes of edema include: eating too much salt, sunburn, heart failure, liver problems and pregnancy. To keep swelling down, your health care provider may recommend keeping your legs raised when sitting, wearing support stockings, limiting how much salt you eat.

definition: Shock is a life-threatening condition that occurs when the body is not getting enough blood flow. Shock requires immediate treatment and can get worse very rapidly. symptoms: The main types of shock include:Cardiogenic shock (due to heart problems) Hypovolemic shock (caused by too little blood volume) Anaphylactic shock (cused by allergic reaction) Septic shock ( due to infections) Neurogenic shock (Caused

If the person is unconscious and unresponsive, does not have a pulse, and an automated external defibrillator (AED) is immediately available - follow the instructions on the AED device. Simple pulmonary eosinophilia is inflammation of the lungs from an increase in eosinophils, a type of white blood cell.
risk_factors: A rare complication of simple pulmonary eosinophilia is a severe type of pneumonia called acute idiopathic eos inophilic pneumonia.

definition: Myocarditis is inflammation of the heart muscle. The condition is called pediatric myocarditis when it occurs in children. Causes Myocarditis is an uncommon disorder.
symptoms: Myocarditis can be hard to diagnose because the signs and symptoms often mimic those of other heart and lung diseases, or a bad case of the flu. If symptoms occur, they may include: Chest pain that may resemble a heart attack. Fatigue or listlessness. Fever and other
diagnosis: A chest x-ray can show enlargement (swelling) of the heart. An electrocardiogram (ECG) may also be done to help make the diagnosis.
treatment: Myocarditis following COVID-19 vaccination has been reported, but is very rare. Other causes of myocarditis include: exposure to chemicals in the environment, such as heavy metals.
risk_factors: Treat conditions that cause myocarditis promptly to reduce the risk of developing the condition.

Drug-induced hypertension is high blood pressure caused by a chemical substance or medicine.
Atrial septal defects are defined as primum or secundum.

Coronary artery spasm is a brief, sudden narrowing of one of these arteries. Causes The spasm often occurs in coronary arteries that have not become hardened due to plaque buildup. These spasms are due to a squeezing of muscles in the artery wall. They most often occur in just one area of the artery. The pain of coronary artery spasm: Often occurs at rest May occur at the same time each day, usually between midnight and 8:00 a.m. Lasts from 5 to 30 minutes The person may lose consciousness. Outlook (Prognosis) Coronary artery spasm is a long-term ( chronic ) condition. Alternative Names Variant angina; Angina - variant; Prinzmetal angina; Vasospastic angina; Chest pain - Prinzmetal Patient Instructions Angina - discharge Angina - what to ask your doctor Angina - when you have chest pain Images Angina Coronary artery spasm Artery cut section Prevention of heart disease
diagnosis: The goal of treatment is to control chest pain and prevent a heart attack. Coronary artery spasm may be diagnosed by tests such as an ECG.
treatment: beta-blockers may make coronary artery spasm worse. They should be used with care.
risk_factors: In many people, coronary artery spasm may occur without any other heart risk factors (such as smoking, diabetes, high blood pressure, and high cholesterol)

definition: Factors that can increase your risk of having this problem include: Smoking High blood pressure Male sex Genetic factors An abdominal aortic aneurysm is most often seen in males over age 60 who have one or more risk factors. When an abdominal aortic aneurysm begins to tear or ruptures, it is a medical emergency. Only about 1 in 5 people survive a ruptured abdominal aneurysm.
symptoms: You may have an abdominal aortic aneurysm that is not causing any symptoms.
risk_factors: An abdominal aortic aneurysm is most often seen in males over age 60 who have one or more risk factors. Factors that can increase your risk of having this problem include: Smoking, high blood pressure, male sex and genetic factors.

Treatment Costochondritis most often goes away on its own in a few days or weeks. Outlook (Prognosis) Costochondritis pain often goes away in a few days or weeks.
symptoms: The most common symptoms of costochondritis are pain and tenderness in the chest. Because the cause is often unknown, there is no known way to prevent it. Contact your provider if you have any of the following symptoms.
treatment: Costochondritis most often goes away on its own in a few days or weeks.

definition: Causes Digitalis toxicity can be caused by high levels of digitalis in the body.
symptoms: Some plants contain chemicals that can cause symptoms similar to digitalis toxicity if they are eaten. Digitalis toxicity symptoms include confusion, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea and blurred vision.
treatment: Digitalis toxicity can be a side effect of digitalis therapy. Digitalis therapy is a form of stem cell therapy.
risk_factors: People may also develop digitalis toxicity if they have other risk factors. A low level of potassium in the body can increase the risk.

definition: Pericarditis is inflammation and swelling of the covering of the heart (pericardium). Late pericarditis: This is also called Dressler syndrome. Tests may include: Cardiac injury markers (CK-MB and troponin may help tell pericarditis from a heart attack) Chest CT scan Chest MRI Chest x-ray Complete blood count (CBC) ECG (electrocardiogram) Echocardiogram ESR (sedimentation rate) or C-reactive protein (measures of inflammation) Treatment The goal of treatment is to make the heart work better and reduce pain and other symptoms.
symptoms: A previous heart attack can put you at higher risk for pericarditis. The goal of treatment is to make the heart work better and reduce pain.
treatment: The health care provider will listen to your heart and lungs with a stethoscope. The first type of pericarditis is more common than the second type.

definition: Severe hypovolemic shock may lead to death, even with immediate medical attention. Possible Complications Complications may include: Kidney damage (may require temporary or permanent use of a kidney dialysis machine) Brain damage Gangrene of arms or legs, sometimes leading to amputation Heart attack Other organ damage Death When to Contact a Medical Professional Hypovolemic shock is a medical emergency.
risk_factors: Hypovolemic shock is a medical emergency. Hypovolemia may cause brain damage,angrene of arms or legs, heart attack, other organ damage and death.

definition: Dilated cardiomyopathy is a condition in which the heart muscle becomes weakened and enlarged. Some health care providers use the term to indicate a specific condition, called idiopathic dilated cardiomyopathy. Alternative Names Cardiomyopathy - dilated; Primary cardiomyopathy; Diabetic cardiomyopathy; Idiopathic cardiomyopathy; Alcoholic cardiomyopathy Images Heart - section through the middle Heart - front view Dilated cardiomyopathy Alcoholic cardiomyopathy
treatment: Some health care providers use the term to indicate a specific condition, called idiopathic dilated cardiomyopathy.

definition: Peripheral artery disease (PAD) is a condition of the blood vessels that supply the legs and feet. People are at higher risk if they have a history of: Abnormal blood cholesterol level Diabetes Heart disease (coronary artery disease) High blood pressure ( hypertension ) Kidney disease involving hemodialysis Smoking Stroke ( cerebrovascular disease ) Symptoms The main symptoms of PAD are pain, achiness, fatigue, burning, or discomfort in the muscles of your feet, calves, or thighs. Alternative Names Peripheral vascular disease; PVD; PAD; Arteriosclerosis obliterans; Blockage of leg arteries; Claudication; Intermittent claudication; Vaso-occlusive disease of the legs; Arterial insufficiency of the legs; Recurrent leg pain and cramping; Calf pain with exercise Patient Instructions Angioplasty and stent placement - peripheral arteries - discharge Antiplatelet drugs - P2Y12 inhibitors Cholesterol and lifestyle Dietary fats explained Fast food tips Foot amputation - discharge How to read food labels Leg amputation - discharge Leg or foot amputation - dressing change Mediterranean diet Peripheral artery bypass - leg - discharge Images Atherosclerosis of the extremities Arterial bypass leg - series
Atherosclerosis is a common disorder. Causes Watch this video about: Atherosclerosis Atherosclerosis often occurs with aging.
symptoms: Atherosclerosis does not cause symptoms until blood flow to part of the body becomes slowed or blocked. Other factors that can contribute to hardening of the arteries include: diabetes, high blood pressure, and being overweight or obese.
treatment: Doppler tests that use ultrasound or sound waves. Magnetic resonance arteriography (MRA), a special type of MRI scan. Special CT scans called CT angiography.
risk_factors: Losing weight if you are overweight and reducing blood sugar if you have diabetes or pre-diabetes can help reduce the risk of developing atherosclerosis.

definition: Causes Thromboangiitis obliterans (Buerger disease) is caused by small blood vessels that become inflamed and swollen. Alternative Names Buerger disease Images Thromboangiitis obliterans Circulatory system
symptoms: Symptoms of thromboangiitis obliterans may go away if the person stops tobacco use. Complications include tissue death and amputation.
diagnosis: There are no blood tests that diagnose thromboangiitis obliterans. There are also no tests to diagnose blood clotting problems.
treatment: There is no cure for thromboangiitis obliterans. There is no treatment for the condition.

definition: As the tear extends along the wall of the aorta, blood can flow in between the layers of the blood vessel wall (dissection). Aortic dissection most often happens because of a tear or damage to the inner wall of the aorta. Treatment Aortic dissection is a life-threatening condition and needs to be treated right away. Dissections that occur in other parts of the aorta (descending) may be managed with surgery or medicines. Outlook (Prognosis) Aortic dissection is life threatening. Possible Complications Aortic dissection may decrease or stop the blood flow to many different parts of the body.
symptoms: If you have symptoms of an aortic dissection or severe chest pain, call 911 or the local emergency number. Go to the emergency room as quickly as possible. Blood work to rule out a heart attack is needed.
diagnosis: Treating and controlling hardening of the arteries (atherosclerosis)Keeping high blood pressure under control, especially if you are at risk for dissection.Taking safety precautions to prevent injuries that can cause dissections.
treatment: Aortic dissection is a life-threatening condition and needs to be treated right away.
risk_factors: Aortic dissection occurs in about 2 out of every 10,000 people. The exact cause is unknown, but more common risks include: aging, trauma to the chest, and high blood pressure.

definition: Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia (PSVT) is episodes of a rapid heart rate that start in a part of the heart above the ventricles. "Paroxysmal" means from time to time.
Atrial fibrillation (Afib) and atrial flutter are common types of abnormal heart rhythms (arrhythmias) which affect the upper chambers (atria) of the heart.

Causes The most common causes of cardiogenic shock are serious heart conditions. Lab tests include: Arterial blood gas Blood chemistry ( chem-7 , chem-20 , electrolytes , lactic acid level) Cardiac enzymes (troponin, CKMB) Complete blood count (CBC) Thyroid stimulating hormone (TSH) Treatment Cardiogenic shock is a medical emergency. Cardiogenic shock is a medical emergency.
symptoms: To diagnose cardiogenic shock, a catheter (tube) may be placed in the lung artery ( right heart catheterization ).
treatment: In the past, the death rate from cardiogenic shock ranged from 80% to 90%.
risk_factors: Cardiogenic shock occurs when the heart is unable to supply as much blood as the body needs. These complications include a large section of heart muscle that no longer moves well or does not move at all.

definition: Alternative Names Wide-complex tachycardia; V tach; Tachycardia - ventricular Patient Instructions Implantable cardioverter defibrillator - discharge Images Implantable cardioverter-defibrillator Implantable cardiac defibrillator
symptoms: Ventricular tachycardia may not cause symptoms in some people. All of these may be signs of ventricular tachycardsia.
treatment: Tests that may be used to detect ventricular tachycardia include:Electrocardiogram (ECG) Holter monitor and electrophysiology study.

definition: Peripartum cardiomyopathy is a rare disorder in which a pregnant woman's heart becomes weakened and enlarged. Peripartum cardiomyopathy is a form of dilated cardiomyopathy in which no other cause of heart weakening can be found. Outlook (Prognosis) There are several possible outcomes in peripartum cardiomyopathy.
risk_factors: Women who develop peripartum cardiomyopathy are at high risk of developing the same problem with future pregnancies.

definition: Restrictive cardiomyopathy refers to a set of changes in how the heart muscle functions. Causes In a case of restrictive cardiomyopathy, the heart muscle is of normal size or slightly enlarged. Restrictive cardiomyopathy is a rare condition. People with restrictive cardiomyopathy may be heart transplant candidates.
symptoms: Restrictive cardiomyopathy may appear similar to constrictive pericarditis. Symptoms of heart failure are most common. Other causes include: Cardiac amyloidosis, endomyocardial fibrosis and Loeffler syndrome.
treatment: Few treatments are known to work well for restrictive cardiomyopathy. Few treatments are currently known to be effective for the condition.

definition: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) is a condition in which the heart muscle becomes thick. In many young adults, the first symptom of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is sudden collapse and possible death. There are different types of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, which have different prognoses.
symptoms: In many young adults, the first symptom of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is sudden collapse and possible death. Contact your provider if you have any symptoms of the disease.
diagnosis: Close family members of people with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy may be screened for the condition.
treatment: Always follow your provider's advice about exercise if you have hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.
risk_factors: People with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy are at higher risk for sudden death than people without the condition.

definition: Most heart attacks are caused by a blood clot that blocks one of the coronary arteries. A heart attack may occur when: A disruption in the plaque occurs. Symptoms A heart attack is a medical emergency. If you have symptoms of a heart attack, call 911 or your local emergency number right away. You are at greatest risk for sudden death in the early hours of a heart attack. Chest pain is the most common symptom of a heart attack. Most people can slowly go back to normal activities after a heart attack.
symptoms: A heart attack is a medical emergency. If you have symptoms of a heart attack, call 911 or your local emergency number right away. Some people (including older adults, people with diabetes, and women) may have little or no chest pain.
treatment: After several days, you will be discharged from the hospital. You will learn how to treat your heart problem and prevent more heart attacks. How well you do after a heart attack depends on several factors.
risk_factors: Many risk factors may lead to the development of plaque buildup. You are at greatest risk for sudden death in the early hours of a heart attack.

definition: Stable angina is chest pain or discomfort that most often occurs with activity or emotional stress. Stable angina is less serious than unstable angina, but it can be very painful or uncomfortable. There are many risk factors for coronary artery disease . The pain of stable angina most often begins slowly and gets worse over the next few minutes before going away.
symptoms: Anything that makes the heart muscle need more oxygen or reduces the amount of oxygen it receives can cause an angina attack. Other causes of angina include:Abnormal heart rhythms (your heart beats very quickly or your heart rhythm is not regular) AnemiaCoronary artery spasm
risk_factors: Stable angina is less serious than unstable angina. It can be very painful or uncomfortable. There are many risk factors for coronary artery disease.

definition: Unstable angina is a condition in which your heart doesn't get enough blood flow and oxygen. Unstable angina is chest pain that is sudden and often gets worse over a short period of time. You may be developing unstable angina if your chest pain: Starts to feel different, is more severe, comes more often, or occurs with less activity or while you are at rest Lasts longer than 15 to 20 minutes Occurs without cause (for example, while you are asleep or sitting quietly) Does not respond well to a medicine called nitroglycerin (especially if this medicine worked to relieve chest pain in the past) Occurs with a drop in blood pressure or shortness of breath Unstable angina is a warning sign that a heart attack may happen soon and needs to be treated right away. The decision to have this surgery depends on: Which arteries are blocked How many arteries are involved Which parts of the coronary arteries are narrowed How severe the narrowings are Outlook (Prognosis) Unstable angina is a sign of more severe heart disease. Alternative Names Accelerating angina; New-onset angina; Angina - unstable; Progressive angina; CAD - unstable angina; Coronary artery disease - unstable angina; Heart disease - unstable angina; Chest pain - unstable angina Patient Instructions Angina - discharge Angina - what to ask your doctor Angina - when you have chest pain Angioplasty and stent - heart - discharge Heart attack – discharge Heart attack - what to ask your provider Images Angina Coronary artery balloon angioplasty - series
symptoms: Unstable angina is chest pain that is sudden and often gets worse over a short period of time. It is a warning sign that a heart attack may happen soon and needs to be treated right away.
risk_factors: People with unstable angina are at higher risk of having a heart attack. Seek medical attention right away if you have new, unexplained chest pain. If you have had angina before, contact your provider.

definition: Chronic venous insufficiency is a long-term condition. A duplex ultrasound exam of your leg may be ordered to: Check how blood flows in the veins Check for other problems with the legs, such as a blood clot Treatment Your provider may suggest that you take the following self-care steps to help manage venous insufficiency : Do not sit or stand for long periods. Outlook (Prognosis) Chronic venous insufficiency tends to get worse over time. Alternative Names Chronic venous stasis; Chronic venous disease; Leg ulcer - venous insufficiency; Varicose veins - venous insufficiency Images Venous insufficiency
symptoms: Your health care provider will do a physical exam and ask about your symptoms and medical history.
treatment: A duplex ultrasound exam of your leg may be ordered to:Check how blood flows in the veins.Check for other problems with the legs, such as a blood clot.

definition: Renovascular hypertension is high blood pressure due to narrowing of the arteries that carry blood to the kidneys.
symptoms: High blood pressure that suddenly gets worse or is hard to control. Kidneys that are not working well (this can start suddenly) narrowing of other arteries in the body. Sudden buildup of fluid in the air sacs of the lungs.

definition: Hepatic ischemia is a condition in which the liver does not get enough blood or oxygen. Causes Low blood pressure from any condition can lead to hepatic ischemia. Outlook (Prognosis) People generally recover if the illness causing hepatic ischemia can be treated.

Fanconi anemia is a rare disease passed down through families (inherited) that mainly affects the bone marrow. A lack of red blood cells may result in fatigue ( anemia ). A bone marrow transplant can cure the blood count problems of Fanconi anemia.
symptoms: People with Fanconi anemia have lower-than-normal numbers of white blood cells, and platelets (cells that help the blood clot) Most people have some of these symptoms: abnormal heart, lungs, and digestive tract.
treatment: Women with Fanconi anemia who become pregnant should be watched carefully by a specialist.
risk_factors: People who have had a successful bone marrow transplant still need regular check-ups. The best bone marrow donor is a brother or sister whose tissue type matches the person affected by Fanconi anemia.

definition: Raynaud phenomenon is a condition in which cold temperatures or strong emotions cause blood vessel spasms. Secondary Raynaud phenomenon is when the condition is linked to other conditions and can occur at any age. People with secondary Raynaud phenomenon are more likely to have pain or tingling in the fingers. Tests that may be done to confirm the diagnosis include: Examination of the blood vessels in the fingertips using a special lens called nailfold capillary microscopy Vascular ultrasound Blood tests to look for arthritic and autoimmune conditions that may cause Raynaud phenomenon Treatment Taking these steps may help control Raynaud phenomenon: Keep the body warm. Alternative Names Raynaud disease; Primary Raynaud; Secondary Raynaud Images Raynaud's phenomenon Systemic lupus erythematosus Circulatory system
symptoms: Common causes of secondary Raynaud phenomenon are: Diseases of the arteries (such as atherosclerosis and Buerger disease) Arthritis and autoimmune conditions. Certain blood disorders, such as cold agglutinin disease or cryoglobulinemia.
diagnosis: Tests that may be done to confirm the diagnosis include:Examination of the blood vessels in the fingertips using a special lens called nailfold capillary microscopyVascular ultrasound. Blood tests to look for arthritic and autoimmune conditions that may cause Raynaud phenomenon.
treatment: Your health care provider can often discover the condition causing Raynaud phenomenon by asking you questions and doing a physical exam.

symptoms: IgA vasculitis may cause purple spots on the skin ( purpura) and bleeding inside the body. In rare cases, kidney problems can also be caused by IgA Vasculitis. Contact your doctor if you develop symptoms that last more than a few days

definition: Outlook (Prognosis) Necrotizing vasculitis can be serious and life-threatening disease.
symptoms: Contact your provider if you have symptoms of necrotizing vasculitis. Complications may include permanent damage to the structure or function of the affected area.
treatment: Most forms of necrotizing vasculitis require long-term follow-up and treatment.

Giant cell arteritis (GCA) is inflammation and damage to the blood vessels that supply blood to the head, neck, upper body and arms. Causes Giant cell arteritis affects medium-to-large arteries.
diagnosis: If the diagnosis of giant cell arteritis is made, in most people a biologic medicine called tocilizumab will be added.

term: high blood pressure in adults – hypertension
definition: If the top blood pressure number is from 120 to 129 mm Hg, and the bottom blood pressure number is less than 80 mm Hg, it is called elevated blood pressure. High blood pressure that is caused by another medical condition or medicine you are taking is called secondary hypertension. Malignant hypertension is a dangerous form of very high blood pressure. Whenever thinking about the best treatment for high blood pressure, you and your provider must consider other factors such as: Your age The medicines you take Your risk of side effects from possible medicines Other medical conditions you may have, such as a history of heart disease, stroke, kidney problems, or diabetes If the top blood pressure number is from 120 to 129 mm Hg, and the bottom blood pressure number is less than 80 mm Hg, you have what is called elevated blood pressure. If your blood pressure is 130/80 or higher, but lower than 140/90 mm Hg, you have Stage 1 high blood pressure. If your blood pressure is 140/90 mm Hg or higher, you have Stage 2 high blood pressure.

Malignant hypertension is very high blood pressure that comes on suddenly and quickly. It also occurs in people with: Collagen vascular disorders (such as systemic lupus erythematosus, systemic sclerosis, and periarteritis nodosa) Kidney problems Pregnancy-induced high blood pressure ( toxemia of pregnancy also called preeclampsia) You are at high risk for malignant hypertension if you smoke and if you have had: Kidney failure Renal hypertension caused by renal artery stenosis Symptoms Symptoms of malignant hypertension include: Blurred vision Change in mental status, such as anxiety , confusion , decreased alertness , decreased ability to concentrate, fatigue , restlessness , sleepiness , or stupor Chest pain (feeling of crushing or pressure) Cough Headache Nausea or vomiting Numbness of the arms, legs, face, or other areas Reduced urine output Seizure Shortness of breath Weakness of the arms, legs, face, or other areas Exams and Tests Malignant hypertension is a medical emergency. Alternative Names Accelerated hypertension; Arteriolar nephrosclerosis; Nephrosclerosis - arteriolar; Hypertension - malignant; High blood pressure - malignant Images Hypertensive kidney
symptoms: Malignant hypertension is a medical emergency. You are at high risk for malignant hypertension if you smoke and if you have had:Kidney failure. Renal hypertension caused by renal artery stenosis.

definition: Sickle cell disease is a disorder passed down through families. Sickle cell disease is inherited from both parents.
symptoms: People with sickle cell trait do not have the symptoms of sicklecell disease. Symptoms include fatigue, paleness,Rapid heart rate, shortness of breath and yellowing of the eyes and skin.
treatment: People with sickle cell disease need ongoing treatment, even when not having a crisis. Blood transfusions (may also be given regularly to prevent stroke)Pain medicines and plenty of fluids are some of the treatments.
risk_factors: People with sickle cell disease should have the following vaccinations to lower the risk for infection.Joining a support group where members share common issues can relieve the stress of a chronic disease.

definition: Chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) is cancer of a type of white blood cells called lymphocytes. Alternative Names CLL; Leukemia - chronic lymphocytic (CLL); Blood cancer - chronic lymphocytic leukemia; Bone marrow cancer - chronic lymphocytic leukemia; Lymphoma - chronic lymphocytic leukemia Patient Instructions Bone marrow transplant - discharge Images Bone marrow aspiration Auer rods Chronic lymphocytic leukemia - microscopic view Antibodies

Immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP) is a bleeding disorder in which the immune system destroys platelets, which are necessary for normal blood clotting. Alternative Names ITP; Immune thrombocytopenia; Bleeding disorder - idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura; Bleeding disorder - ITP; Autoimmune - ITP; Low platelet count - ITP Images Blood cells

Hemophilia refers to a group of bleeding disorders in which blood clotting takes a longer time than normal. Hemophilia is caused by the lack of clotting factor VIII or IX in the blood. Symptoms The main symptom of hemophilia is bleeding. Hemophilia can be mild, moderate, or severe. Outlook (Prognosis) Most people with hemophilia are able to do normal activities.
symptoms: The main symptom of hemophilia is bleeding. The main symptom is bleeding, which is a sign of the condition.
diagnosis: Most often, hemophilia is diagnosed after a person has an abnormal bleeding episode.
risk_factors: Hemophilia is caused by the lack of clotting factor VIII or IX in the blood. You may have a higher chance of excess bleeding if one or more of these factors are missing.

definition: Hemophilia A is a hereditary bleeding disorder caused by a lack of blood clotting factor VIII. Hemophilia A is the result of the body not making enough factor VIII. Hemophilia A is caused by an inherited X-linked recessive trait, with the variant gene located on the X chromosome. All female children of men with hemophilia carry the variant gene whereas male children do not.
symptoms: People with hemophilia A can be taught to give factor VIII concentrates at home at the first signs of bleeding.
diagnosis: Tests to diagnose hemophilia A include: Prothrombin time (PT), Partial thromboplastin time ( PTT) and serum factor VIII activity.
treatment: With treatment, most people with hemophilia A are able to lead a fairly normal life.
risk_factors: Hemophilia A is a hereditary bleeding disorder caused by a lack of blood clotting factor VIII. If the factor VIII gene is missing on a boy's X chromosome, he will have hemophili A. For this reason, most people with hemophiles A are male.

definition: Hemophilia B is a hereditary bleeding disorder caused by a lack of blood clotting factor IX. Hemophilia B is the result of the body not making enough factor IX. Hemophilia B is caused by an inherited X-linked recessive trait, with the variant gene located on the X chromosome. If the factor IX gene is missing on a boy's X chromosome, he will have Hemophilia B. For this reason, most people with hemophilia B are male. Alternative Names Christmas disease; Factor IX hemophilia; Bleeding disorder - hemophilia B Images X-linked recessive genetic defects - how boys are affected X-linked recessive genetic defects - how girls are affected X-linked recessive genetic defects Blood cells Blood clots
symptoms: Risk factors for hemophilia B include: Family history of bleeding and being male. Genetic counseling may be recommended.
diagnosis: Tests to diagnose hemophilia B include: Partial thromboplastin time (PTT) Prothrombin time ( PT) Serum factor IX activity.
treatment: With treatment, most people with hemophilia B are able to lead a fairly normal life.
risk_factors: Hemophilia B is a hereditary bleeding disorder caused by a lack of blood clotting factor IX. If the factor IX gene is missing on a boy's X chromosome, he will have Hemophili B. For this reason, most people with hemophiliaB are male.

definition: Cryoglobulinemia is the presence of abnormal proteins in the blood. They are grouped based on the type of antibody that is produced: Type I Type II Type III Type I cryoglobulinemia is most often related to cancer of the blood or immune systems. Types II and III are also referred to as mixed cryoglobulinemia . Severe cryoglobulinemia vasculitis involves vital organs or large areas of skin. Images Cryoglobulinemia of the fingers Cryoglobulinemia - fingers Blood cells
symptoms: Other conditions that may be related to cryoglobulinemia include: leukemia, multiple myeloma, rheumatoid arthritis and systemic lupus erythematosus.
treatment: MIXED CRYOGLOBULINEMIA (TYPES II AND III) can often be treated by taking steps to deal with the underlying cause.

definition: Acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) is a fast-growing cancer of a type of white blood cells called lymphocytes.

Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is cancer that starts inside bone marrow. Essential thrombocythemia (ET) is a condition in which the bone marrow produces too many platelets.

Von Willebrand disease is the most common hereditary bleeding disorder . Causes Von Willebrand disease is caused by a deficiency or poor functioning of von Willebrand factor. Alternative Names Bleeding disorder - von Willebrand Images Blood clot formation Blood clots
symptoms: Most women with heavy or prolonged menstrual bleeding do not have von Willebrand disease. Symptoms may include: Abnormal menstrual bleeding, bleeding of the gums and bruising.
diagnosis: Von Willebrand disease may be hard to diagnose. Exams and Tests can help diagnose the disease.
risk_factors: Von Willebrand disease is caused by a deficiency or poor functioning of vonWillebrand factor. Low von Wille Brand factor levels and bleeding do not always mean you have von WilLEbrand disease.

symptoms: Using medicines as directed can reduce the risk for drug-related acquired platelet function defects.

definition: Alternative Names Proconvertin deficiency; Extrinsic factor deficiency; Serum prothrombin conversion accelerator deficiency; Alexander disease Images Blood clot formation Blood clots
symptoms: Bleeding can be caused by: low vitamin K (some babies are born with vitamin K deficiency) Severe liver disease (anticoagulants such as warfarin) or clotting problems.
treatment: More information and support for people with Factor VII deficiency and their families can be found at: National Hemophilia Foundation -- www.hemophilia.org/community-resources. National Organization for Rare Disorders -- rarediseases.org /factor-vii-deficiency.
risk_factors: Factor VII deficiency runs in families (inherited) and is very rare. It can also be due to another condition or use of certain medicines. This is called acquired factor VII deficiency.

definition: Factor V deficiency is a bleeding disorder that is passed down through families. Factor V deficiency is caused by a lack of factor V. When certain blood clotting factors are low or missing, your blood does not clot properly. Factor V deficiency is rare. In the inherited form of factor V deficiency, a family history of a bleeding disorder is a risk factor. Alternative Names Parahemophilia; Owren disease; Bleeding disorder - factor V deficiency Images Blood clot formation Blood clots
symptoms: You will be given fresh blood plasma or fresh frozen plasma infusions during a bleeding episode or after surgery. Other symptoms can include: bleeding into the skin and bleeding of the gums.
risk_factors: Factor V deficiency is a bleeding disorder that is passed down through families. When certain blood clotting factors are low or missing, your blood does not clot properly. In the inherited form of factor V deficiency, a family history of a bleeding disorders is a risk factor.

definition: Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP) is a blood disorder in which platelet clumps form in small blood vessels. Possible Complications Complications may include: Kidney failure Low platelet count (thrombocytopenia) Low red blood cell count (caused by the premature breakdown of red blood cells) Nervous system problems Severe bleeding (hemorrhage) Stroke When to Contact a Medical Professional Contact your health care provider if you have any unexplained bleeding.

Factor X deficiency is often caused by an inherited defect in the factor X gene. This is called inherited factor X deficiency. Factor X deficiency can also be due to another condition or use of certain medicines. Inherited factor X deficiency is a lifelong condition. The outlook for acquired factor X deficiency depends on the cause.
diagnosis: Women with factor X deficiency may first be diagnosed when they have very heavy menstrual bleeding and bleeding after childbirth. Some newborns are born with vitamin K deficiency.
treatment: More information and support for people with factor X deficiency and their families can be found at: National Hemophilia Foundation -- www.hemophilia.org/community-resources. National Organization for Rare Disorders -- rarediseases.org / factor-x-deficiency.
risk_factors: Factor X deficiency is often caused by an inherited defect in the factor X gene. This is called inherited factor X deficiency. It can also be due to another condition or use of certain medicines.

definition: Aplastic anemia is a condition in which the bone marrow does not make enough blood cells. Causes Aplastic anemia results from damage to the blood stem cells. In this case, the disorder is called idiopathic aplastic anemia. Low red cell count (anemia) can cause: Fatigue Pallor (paleness) Rapid heart rate Shortness of breath with exercise Weakness Lightheadedness upon standing Low white cell count (leukopenia) causes an increased risk for infection. Symptoms include: Bleeding gums Easy bruising Nose bleeds Rash, small pinpoint red marks on the skin (petechiae) Frequent or severe infections (less common) Exams and Tests Blood tests will show: Low red blood cell count (anemia) Low white blood cell count (leukopenia) Low reticulocyte count (reticulocytes are the youngest red blood cells) Low platelet count (thrombocytopenia) A bone marrow biopsy shows fewer-than-normal blood cells and an increased amount of fat. Alternative Names Hypoplastic anemia; Bone marrow failure - aplastic anemia Patient Instructions Bone marrow transplant - discharge Images Bone marrow aspiration
symptoms: Mild cases of aplastic anemia that do not have symptoms may not require treatment.
treatment: Aplastic anemia can be caused by: Use of certain medicines or exposure to toxic chemicals. Exposure to radiation or chemotherapy.Autoimmune disorders.Pregnancy.Viruses.

definition: Chemotherapy drugs and a seizure medicine called valproic acid may lead to this problem.

treatment: Chemotherapy drugs and a seizure medicine called valproic acid may lead to this problem.

Different types of anemia include: Anemia due to vitamin B12 deficiency Anemia due to folate (folic acid) deficiency Anemia due to iron deficiency Anemia of chronic disease Hemolytic anemia Idiopathic aplastic anemia Megaloblastic anemia Pernicious anemia Sickle cell anemia Thalassemia Iron deficiency anemia is the most common type of anemia. People with anemia do not have enough hemoglobin.
symptoms: The body may not have enough of these nutrients due to: changes in the lining of the stomach or intestines that affect how well nutrients are absorbed. Long-term (chronic) diseases such as chronic kidney disease, cancer, ulcerative colitis , or rheumatoid
diagnosis: Blood tests used to diagnose some common types of anemia may include: blood levels of iron, vitamin B12, folic acid, and other vitamins and minerals.Complete blood count.Reticulocyte count.
treatment: Severe anemia can cause low oxygen levels in vital organs such as the heart, and can lead to heart failure. Treatment should be directed at the cause of the anemia.

definition: Outlook (Prognosis) Most people with hereditary elliptocytosis have no problems.

symptoms: Anemia of chronic disease is often mild. Some conditions that can lead to ACD include: Autoimmune disorders, cancer and long-term infections.

symptoms: When to Contact a Medical ProfessionalContact your health care provider if you develop symptoms of hemolytic anemia.

definition: Hemoglobin C disease is a blood disorder passed down through families. Outlook (Prognosis) People with hemoglobin C disease can expect to lead a normal life.
symptoms: Contact your health care provider if you have symptoms of hemoglobin C disease. Complications may include: Anemia,Gallbladder disease,Enlargement of the spleen.

The breakdown of fibrin (fibrinolysis) can be due to: Bacterial infections Cancer Intense exercise Not enough oxygen to tissues Your health care provider may give you medicines to help blood clots break down more quickly.
treatment: Your health care provider may give you medicines to help blood clots break down more quickly. The breakdown of fibrin (fibrinolysis) can be due to: bacterial infections, cancer, intense exercise and not enough oxygen to tissues.

Iron deficiency anemia occurs when your body does not have enough iron. Iron deficiency anemia is the most common form of anemia. Iron deficiency anemia develops when your body's iron stores run low.
symptoms: Iron deficiency anemia can be caused by bleeding. Symptoms may include: Headaches, dizziness, palpitations, thirst, fatigue, and hair loss.

definition: Thrombocytopenia means there is an abnormally low amount of platelets. Alternative Names Low platelet count - thrombocytopenia

Thalassemia is a blood disorder passed down through families (inherited) in which the body makes an abnormal form or inadequate amount of hemoglobin. Causes Hemoglobin is made of two proteins: Alpha globin Beta globin Thalassemia occurs when there is a variant in a gene that helps control production of one of these proteins. Beta thalassemias occur most often in people of Mediterranean origin. There are many forms of thalassemia. Both alpha and beta thalassemia include the following two forms: Thalassemia major Thalassemia minor You must inherit the variant gene from both parents to develop thalassemia major. Children born with beta thalassemia major (Cooley anemia) are normal at birth, but develop severe anemia during the first year of life. A test called hemoglobin electrophoresis shows the presence of an abnormal form of hemoglobin and can detect beta thalassemia. Less severe forms of thalassemia often do not shorten lifespan. Possible Complications Untreated, thalassemia major leads to heart failure and liver problems.
symptoms: The most severe form of alpha thalassemia major causes stillbirth (death of the unborn baby during birth or the late stages of pregnancy) Other symptoms can include: bone deformities in the face, fatigue, growth failure, and shortness of breath.
treatment: Treatment for thalassemia major often involves regular blood transfusions and folate supplements.
risk_factors: Untreated, thalassemia major leads to heart failure and liver problems.

definition: Alternative Names Leukemic reticuloendotheliosis; HCL; Leukemia - hairy cell Images Bone marrow aspiration Hairy cell leukemia - microscopic view Enlarged spleen
risk_factors: The low blood counts caused by hairy cell leukemia can lead to: infections, fatigue and excessive bleeding. Call your provider if you have major bleeding.

definition: Malaria is a parasitic disease that involves high fevers, shaking chills, flu-like symptoms, and anemia . Causes Malaria is caused by a parasite. In some areas of the world, mosquitoes that carry malaria have developed resistance to insecticides. Falciparum malaria is becoming increasingly resistant to anti-malarial medicines. Recommended medicines include mefloquine, atovaquone/proguanil (Malarone), and doxycycline.
symptoms: Malaria is a parasitic disease that involves high fevers, shaking chills, flu-like symptoms, and anemia. Malaria can also be transmitted from a mother to her unborn baby (congenitally) and by blood transfusions.
diagnosis: Malaria, especially falciparum malaria, is a medical emergency that requires a hospital stay. Tests that are done include:Rapid diagnostic tests, which are becoming more common.
treatment: Outcome is expected to be good in most cases of malaria with treatment, but poor in falciparum infection with complications. Health problems that may result from malaria include:Brain infection, kidney failure, liver failure and meningitis.

definition: Any type of bacteria can cause septic shock.
symptoms: Septic shock can affect any part of the body, including the heart, brain, kidneys, liver, and intestines. Go directly to an emergency department if you develop symptoms of septic shock.
treatment: Septic shock is a medical emergency. Septic shock should be treated as soon as possible.

definition: Subarachnoid hemorrhage is bleeding in the area between the brain and the thin tissues that cover the brain. Subarachnoid bleeding is an emergency and prompt medical attention is needed. Among the young, the most common injury leading to subarachnoid hemorrhage is motor vehicle crashes. Prevention The following measures may help prevent subarachnoid hemorrhage: Stopping smoking Treating high blood pressure Identifying and successfully treating an aneurysm Not using illicit drugs Alternative Names Hemorrhage - subarachnoid; Subarachnoid bleeding Patient Instructions Headache - what to ask your doctor
symptoms: How well a person with subarachnoid hemorrhage does depends on a number of different factors, including location and amount of bleeding. The person will be told to avoid activities that can increase pressure inside the head.

Arterial insufficiency is any condition that slows or stops the flow of blood through your arteries. Causes One of the most common causes of arterial insufficiency is atherosclerosis or "hardening of the arteries.

A stroke occurs when blood flow to a part of the brain stops. A stroke is sometimes called a "brain attack." If blood flow is cut off for longer than a few seconds, the brain cannot get nutrients and oxygen. This is called a thrombotic stroke . Very high blood pressure may cause blood vessels to burst, leading to hemorrhagic stroke. An ischemic stroke can develop bleeding and become a hemorrhagic stroke. High blood pressure is the main risk factor for strokes . Your provider and nurses will repeat this exam over time to see if your stroke is getting worse or improving. You may have the following tests to help find the type, location, and cause of the stroke and rule out other problems: CT scan of the brain to determine if there is any bleeding MRI of the brain to determine the location of the stroke Angiogram of the head to look for a blood vessel that is blocked or bleeding Carotid duplex (ultrasound) to see if the carotid arteries in your neck have narrowed Echocardiogram to see if the stroke could have been caused by a blood clot from the heart Magnetic resonance angiography (MRA) or CT angiography to check for abnormal blood vessels in the brain Other tests include: Blood tests Electroencephalogram (EEG) to determine if there are seizures Electrocardiogram (ECG) and heart rhythm monitoring Treatment A stroke is a medical emergency. If the stroke is caused by a blood clot, a clot-busting medicine may be given to dissolve the clot. Many people develop depression after a stroke. When to Contact a Medical Professional Stroke is a medical emergency that needs to be treated right away.
symptoms: African Americans are more likely to die of a stroke. Other major risk factors are:Irregular heartbeat, called atrial fibrillation, diabetes, and family history of stroke.
treatment: A stroke is a medical emergency. The goal of treatment after a stroke is to help you recover as much function as possible and prevent future strokes.
risk_factors: High blood pressure is the main risk factor for strokes. This can slow down recovery but is also a very treatable complication. The risk for a second stroke is highest during the weeks or months after the first stroke.

definition: A transient ischemic attack (TIA) occurs when blood flow to a part of the brain stops for a brief time.
symptoms: A transient ischemic attack is a warning sign that a true stroke may happen in the future (often near future) if something is not done to prevent it.
